title: Python: adapters
summary: The 22 adapter files (4,103 lines) pass the service's ruff, format and mypy-strict gates and contain practices worth spreading: failure codes that say whether an external write certainly did not happen, injectable transports and resolvers tested with sockets blocked, per-attempt credentials, a fail-closed OpenRouter factory, one URL guard and a fenced checkpointer. The cost sits in three hotspots. Each tool module is one factory closure of 68 to 226 lines. github_pull_request_tool's complexity of 37 is the sum of 13 nested functions, the largest of which is 62 lines. Request, status and reply handling is re-implemented for each provider and has drifted: three refused-status sets, two UnclearReply classes, six client constructors with different proxy and timeout defaults, and untyped JSON replies. loop_middleware.py (674 lines) holds model-route and stop policy that application code imports back; its _admitted_call passes state through four lists and treats any ValueError as a lost lease. browser_executor.py packs five concerns into one file covered by the qualification fingerprint. Two defects were reproduced in memory. First, the live-result tap raises on malformed save_artifact arguments, which stops a paid reply as partial_stream or uncertain_acceptance, depending on when the tap flushes. Second, a date-only `since` crashes github_list_pull_requests. Reading also found three more problems: the PR connector resets approvals with inline SQL outside a transaction and without the lease, the URL guard lets httpx resolve a name again after checking it (certificate verification, not the guard, is what stops a rebound request), and the worker converts reported charges with float arithmetic. Apart from those two reproductions, the review is static.

scores.why: Ruff, format and mypy strict pass on all 22 files. But some DH-06 requirements are met unevenly (lease-fenced writes, trust-boundary validation, client lifecycles, exact money), and the rule path scopes miss loop_middleware.

Approval state is written from a GitHub adapter, application imports loop policy back from adapters, and a 500-line fingerprinted browser module all add recurring cost. models/, url_guard and checkpoints are cohesive.
There are seven factory closures of 68 to 226 lines and two files over 300 lines, though each nested handler is small (the largest, open_pull_request, is 62 lines).
Handlers are mostly single-purpose. _admitted_call passes state through four mutable lists, and open_pull_request chains six steps.
The flat adapters/ folder mixes providers, LangChain middleware, a Docker executor and a sidecar. DH-03's graphs/ and adapters/persistence/ don't exist.

Per-attempt keys, injected transports and certainty-aware failures are strong. Against that, the URL guard resolves DNS twice, clients are built six ways, and GitHub reads resolve the target per request.
Module docstrings cite decisions and comments explain why. Two docstrings promise more than the code delivers (result_stream, url_guard).
mypy strict passes, but middleware hooks, connections and every provider reply are Any, and ToolDefinition keywords are passed through dict[str, Any] splats.
Typed codes with explicit certainty are a model for the repository. They are undercut by a tap that turns parse errors into uncertain calls, ValueError used as a signal, and drifting status maps.
Every adapter test uses fake transports with sockets blocked. There are no fast tests for the PR connector, the gateway middleware or storage, and the parsers have no malformed-input cases.
Small, well-commented helpers surround three hotspots (the PR connector, the loop middleware and the browser executor) that need planned refactors.

strengths.title: Failure codes that state certainty
strengths.evidence: Effectful adapters raise ToolFailed only when the destination proves nothing happened, and leave every other outcome unknown for a readback. See services/agent/src/autobots/adapters/github_issues.py:44-45 and 180-186 (connection never opened, the refused set, any other status is UnclearReply) and github_pulls.py:175-184. Readbacks raise NotDelivered only after the settle waits (github_issues.py:48-52, 189-212). The gateway contract they follow is written at application/tool_gateway.py:24-29.

strengths.title: Every network seam is injectable, and tests run with sockets blocked
strengths.evidence: Transports, resolvers, environ, clocks and waits are parameters: tavily.py:42-46, jina.py:42-46, market_data.py:78-80, github_issues.py:145-150, url_guard.py:90-98 and egress_proxy.py:137-143. services/agent/tests/conftest.py:22-27 blocks connect and getaddrinfo for the whole session, and the adapter tests use httpx.MockTransport.

strengths.title: Credentials live for one attempt and one client
strengths.evidence: provider_http.py:1-8 and 28-40 resolve a key per attempt and name only the credential on failure. github_issues.py:75-98 pins writes and readbacks to the repository the approval recorded. models/factory.py:90-107 hands a SecretStr to one prepared client.

strengths.title: A fail-closed OpenRouter factory and catalog
strengths.evidence: models/factory.py:22-64 refuses forbidden or unsupported options instead of dropping them. Lines 110-115 turn SDK retries off and set a timeout above the loop's bound, pinned by services/agent/tests/test_model_attempts.py:297-298. models/catalog.py:45-62 and 133-149 price with Decimal ceilings and refuse stale, future-dated, ambiguous or drifted entries without substituting a model.

strengths.title: One URL guard with typed refusals, and a proxy that pins its address
strengths.evidence: url_guard.py:51-79 and 107-153 check https only, userinfo, length, public DNS answers, every redirect, size and time, each with a typed code. Tavily, Jina and store_remote_file share the guard. The egress proxy connects to the address it checked (egress_proxy.py:73-99, 156-162).

strengths.title: Streaming without weakening tool-call validation
strengths.evidence: loop_middleware.py:175-205 re-parses each streamed tool call so a cut-off argument stays an invalid call (tested at services/agent/tests/test_result_stream.py:159-166). tavily.py:37-38 and 53 merge the no-inference options last, so no caller can turn provider-side generation on.

strengths.title: Comments that record why, citing the decision
strengths.evidence: github_issues.py:48-52 explains the readback waits by pointing to a live run; models/catalog.py:13-17 states what RESERVED_PROMPT_TOKENS can't catch; models/factory.py:110-115 explains why SDK retries are off; url_guard.py:130-132 explains why the peer is checked again; browser_executor.py:267 records a Docker counting quirk.

strengths.title: A fenced checkpointer tied to its qualified stack
strengths.evidence: checkpoints.py:59-77 sets the lease generation on the checkpointer's own connection so the database refuses stale writes. Lines 21-47 fingerprint the adapter release, its migrations and the SQL it relies on.

findings.title: The live-result tap's JSON reader can stop a paid reply as partial_stream or uncertain_acceptance

locations.note: flush parses every save_artifact call before checking its path, and nothing catches the parser
_read_string raises through json.loads (66, 91) and int(..., 16) (73)
Docstring: a failure here never stops the run
Only send failures are caught
_streamed turns any exception after the first chunk into PARTIAL_STREAM
Every goal run sets a tap
Only a failing send is tested

findings.evidence:
flush parses each save_artifact call before checking its path, and nothing catches the parser. _streamed then converts any exception raised after the first chunk:
```
call.changed = False
fields, growing = partial_object(call.arguments)        # result_stream.py:201-202
...
except Exception:
    if assembled is not None:
        raise ProviderFailure(FailureClass.PARTIAL_STREAM) from None   # loop_middleware.py:163-165
```
Reproduced in memory with the service venv, using a fake stream and a fake notify and no database or network. A save_artifact call whose content holds a raw newline gives one invalid tool call without a tap. With a tap it gives ProviderFailure(partial_stream) when the bad text arrives in a feed that flushes, and a bare JSONDecodeError out of tap.finish() in the finally clause when it arrives inside the 0.15-second coalescing window; dispatch then classifies that one as uncertain_acceptance. partial_object also raises JSONDecodeError on an invalid escape such as backslash-q, and ValueError on backslash-u followed by non-hex characters.
findings.impact: Every goal run sets a tap. Without the tap, a reply with a malformed tool call gets an invalid-tool-call message and the model can try again. With the tap, the call is recorded as uncertain (partial_stream or uncertain_acceptance, depending on when the tap flushes): the reservation stays open for reconciliation and the run stops. The module's own invariant, 'A failure here never stops the run', holds only for send failures. Parsing happens before the outputs/ path check, so any save_artifact call can trigger it.
findings.recommendation: Make the tap total. In flush, catch ValueError (JSONDecodeError is a subclass) around partial_object and stop streaming that call. In _streamed, call tap.begin, feed and finish through a helper that logs result_text.unavailable once, disables the tap and never raises. Add tests with a tap present for a raw control character, an invalid escape and a bad unicode escape; each should assert that the reply comes back with an invalid tool call. Add one more test showing that an error in finish() doesn't escape. Reword the 'tolerant reader' comment at line 48 to say it tolerates incomplete input, not malformed input.
findings.sketch:
# result_stream.py
async def flush(self) -> None:
    for call in self._calls.values():
        if call.name != RESULT_TOOL or not call.changed or call.unreadable:
            continue
        call.changed = False
        try:
            fields, growing = partial_object(call.arguments)
        except ValueError:      # malformed, not just incomplete: the stored artifact stays the record
            call.unreadable = True
            continue
        ...
# loop_middleware._streamed
await _tap_safely(tap.feed, chunk)   # any Exception: logged once, tap disabled, nothing raised
findings.ruleCheck: Decision 0022 D4 and US-15.24 (the module docstring) say a tap failure never stops the run; the fix enforces that. Real stream failures keep the model-gateway classification (partial_stream, reconciled, not retried), and tests stay on fake streams (python-worker rule).
findings.verifierNote: Reproduced both paths in memory with fakes: a parse error during feed gives partial_stream, and one inside finish() escapes as JSONDecodeError that dispatch classifies uncertain_acceptance; severity stays high.

findings.title: The pull-request connector rewrites approval state with inline SQL, outside a transaction and without the lease

locations.note: approved_detail and return_to_review: four writes, no transaction, no lease check
Called when the base branch moved
The owning module's re-request, inside approval_gate's transaction (109)
DEFAULT_TTL_SECONDS = 86_400; the adapter hard-codes interval '1 day'
Handler-side writes take hold_lease inside a transaction
append_event is two statements; the gapless sequence relies on the caller's transaction
The step connection the tool context runs on is autocommit

findings.evidence:
When the base has moved, return_to_review runs four separate statements on the worker's autocommit connection, with no hold_lease or hold_running first:
```
await context.connection.execute(
    "update app_private.tool_receipts set reconciled_at = now() where operation_id = %s", ...)
cursor = await context.connection.execute(
    "update public.approval_requests set status = 'pending', decided_by = null, "
    "decided_at = null, review_detail = %s, "
    "expires_at = clock_timestamp() + interval '1 day' " ...)
```
It then calls append_event, which updates runs.event_sequence and inserts into run_events. Elsewhere, a handler-side write takes the lease inside a transaction (tools.py:76-77), and approval_gate's own re-request runs in one transaction with a TTL parameter.
findings.impact: The approvals state machine is split between application/approvals.py and a GitHub adapter. Each statement commits on its own. A crash or cancel between them can leave the receipt reconciled while the approval stays approved, or skip a run_events sequence number that append_event documents as gapless. A worker that lost its lease during the GitHub reads can still reset a person's decision, which the python-worker rule forbids. The TTL duplicates DEFAULT_TTL_SECONDS, and any new approval column or rule must also be remembered in this adapter.
findings.recommendation: Move the transition into application/approvals.py as one function that runs in a single transaction. It takes the lease first (hold_lease, as write_run_file does), reconciles the receipt, resets the approval with the new detail and the standard TTL, and appends approval.requested. tool_gateway imports approvals, so move hold_lease into application/worker_leases.py to avoid an import cycle. The adapter keeps only the reads that build the new diff, then raises base_moved. Move approved_detail and github_issues.approved_repository next to the new function as read helpers. Before the move, add a stale-generation case to tests/db/pull_request_check.py next to its base-moved and re-approval cases.
findings.sketch:
# application/worker_leases.py (moved from tool_gateway, which imports approvals)
async def hold_lease(connection, run_id: UUID, generation: int) -> None: ...

# application/approvals.py
async def rerequest_review(connection, *, run_id: UUID, generation: int, operation_id: str,
                           tool_id: str, detail: dict[str, Any],
                           ttl_seconds: int = DEFAULT_TTL_SECONDS) -> None:
    """Decision 0022 D15: nothing was sent, so a person sees the diff against the new head."""
    async with connection.transaction():
        await hold_lease(connection, run_id, generation)
        await _mark_receipt_reconciled(connection, operation_id)
        approval_id = await _reset_to_pending(connection, operation_id, detail, ttl_seconds)
        await append_event(connection, run_id, _requested(approval_id, tool_id))

async def approved_review_detail(connection, operation_id: str) -> dict[str, Any]: ...

# adapters/github/pulls.py, when the base moved
await rerequest_review(ctx.connection, run_id=ctx.scope.run_id, generation=ctx.scope.generation, ...)
raise ToolFailed("base_moved")
findings.ruleCheck: python-worker rule: enforce leases and fencing on product writes and persist outbox events. SP-010: transitions need guards and an atomic update with their event. Decision 0022 D15's behavior (return to pending with a diff against the new head) is kept, only moved into the module that owns approvals. Nothing in the approval binding is relaxed.
findings.verifierNote: Four unfenced autocommit statements and the hard-coded day confirmed; the tool context's step connection is opened autocommit at operations/worker.py:135-136, not line 79 (the heartbeat), so that location was corrected.

findings.title: Each tool module is one factory closure of 68 to 226 lines, which hides its helpers from per-function metrics and tests

locations.note: 13 nested functions; C901 37 and 92 statements are their sum; largest handler is open_pull_request at 186-247
5 nested handlers; C901 18
7 nested functions; tool() at 148 takes 9 positional arguments
C901 15 across two handlers
Three 'if version == 2' expressions and a getattr on the input union (173)
common: dict[str, Any] splatted into ToolDefinition; also jina.py:112, market_data.py:167, remote_files.py:74

findings.evidence:
```
def github_pull_request_tool(
    transport: httpx.AsyncBaseTransport | None = None,
    environ: Mapping[str, str] = os.environ,
) -> ToolDefinition:
    async def read(http: httpx.AsyncClient, path: str, params: Any = None) -> httpx.Response:
    ...                                     # 12 more nested functions, 226 lines in all
GITHUB_PULL_REQUEST = github_pull_request_tool()
```
The same shape appears in github_read_tools (212 lines), tavily_tools (188), market_tools (134), jina_tools (111), github_issue_tool (95) and store_remote_file_tool (68), 1,034 lines in all. Ruff's C901 counts nested bodies, so the scores 37, 18, 15 and 12 are totals for each container. An AST count per closure puts the largest handlers at open_pull_request (62 lines), workflow_runs (48) and inflation (47).
findings.impact: Helpers such as head_of, content_at, existing and write can't be imported or tested on their own, and handlers are reached only by building the whole definition with a fake transport, as test_github_reads.py does. The riskiest connector, the PR one, is exercised only by the db profile. Shared state (transport, environ) is captured implicitly, so each module re-creates its own client, error and parsing helpers; the drift is described in the next findings. Complexity limits can't be applied per handler: the metric flags containers while the real hotspot, open_pull_request, stays hidden. ToolDefinition keywords passed through dict[str, Any] escape mypy.
findings.recommendation: Adopt one shape for tool adapters and migrate module by module, starting with the PR connector behind new fast tests. The shape has four parts. (1) A small frozen connector per provider owns transport and environ and opens one client per attempt. (2) Handlers are module-level functions taking (api, arguments, context), so each can be tested directly. (3) A typed, keyword-only builder replaces the dict splats and Tavily's positional tool(). (4) Exported singletons, tool IDs, versions and schemas stay unchanged.
findings.sketch:
adapters/github/

                  async with connector.attempt(ctx) as api   # target, token, one client per attempt
                class GithubApi: read(path, params) / write(path, payload)   # one status and error table
  issues.py     create_issue(api, args, ctx), find_issue(api, ctx), ISSUE_VERSIONS = {1: ..., 2: ...}
  pulls.py      review_detail(api, args); open_pull_request(api, args, ctx):
                  _check_base -> _commit_files (tree, commit, ref) -> _find_open_pull or _open_pull
  reads.py      list_pull_requests, list_workflow_runs, search_issues, read_file: (api, args)
adapters/web/tavily.py, jina.py; adapters/market/yahoo.py, world_bank.py   # same three parts
adapters/tool_builders.py  def read_only_tool(*, tool_id, title, description, input_model,
                           output_model, handler, ...) -> ToolDefinition   # typed, keyword-only
GITHUB_READ_TOOLS = github_read_tools()   # exported names, tool IDs and versions unchanged
findings.ruleCheck: Tool IDs, versions, input and output models and public fields stay identical, so version-pinned grants and catalogs are unaffected. Keys and targets are still resolved per attempt (PK-01, Decisions 0017, 0024 and 0025). No generated contract changes.
findings.verifierNote: Closure sizes, nesting and C901 totals (37, 18, 15, 15, 12) confirmed with ast and ruff; handlers are already unit-tested through the built definitions, so severity lowered to medium and the impact reworded.

findings.title: Status and error mapping is copied per provider and has drifted

locations.note: _REFUSED without 409
First UnclearReply
_REFUSED with 409, and a second UnclearReply
Any HTTPError becomes destination_unreachable; any non-200, 5xx included, becomes github_refused_N
_REFUSED without 400; 5xx becomes github_unavailable
failure_for: 429 becomes rate_limited; GitHub doesn't use it
Re-implements client, transport-error, status and JSON mapping; also jina.py:47-63 and market_data.py:83-99

findings.evidence:
```
_REFUSED = frozenset({400, 401, 403, 404, 410, 422, 429})        # github_issues.py:45
_REFUSED = frozenset({400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 410, 422, 429})   # github_pulls.py:45
_REFUSED = frozenset({401, 403, 404, 410, 422, 429})             # github_reads.py:40
raise ToolFailed(f"github_refused_{reply.status_code}")  # github_pulls.py:83, any non-200 incl. 5xx
raise ToolFailed("github_unavailable")                   # github_reads.py:57, the same 5xx
if status == 429: return ToolFailed("rate_limited")      # provider_http.py:63-64
```
Counted by grep: four status-to-code mappings (three _REFUSED sets and failure_for), two identical UnclearReply classes, and eight 'except httpx' blocks in six tool modules.
findings.impact: The model and the receipts see different codes for the same condition. A GitHub 429 is github_refused_429 while Tavily's is rate_limited. A GitHub 503 is github_refused_503 in the PR connector and github_unavailable in the read tools. Each new connector copies one of the variants, and two UnclearReply classes with one meaning leave readers unsure which one to raise.
findings.recommendation: Give the mechanics one home in provider_http (or a new adapters/http module): one UnclearReply, a read helper (transport error becomes ToolFailed(unreachable), a non-2xx status a mapped code, bad JSON malformed) and a write helper (only connect errors and statuses that prove nothing was written become ToolFailed; anything unclear raises UnclearReply). Keep each destination's write-refused set in one named constant, with a comment on why each status proves no write (409 for refs). Make every GitHub read map 5xx the same way.
findings.sketch:
# adapters/provider_http.py
class UnclearReply(Exception): ...                       # one, shared by every write
async def read_json(client, path, *, params=None, code_for=failure_for) -> Any
async def write_json(client, path, payload, *, refused: frozenset[int], code_for) -> Any
# adapters/github/connector.py
GITHUB_WRITE_REFUSED = frozenset({...})   # why each status proves nothing was created
def github_code(status: int) -> str       # one read mapping: 5xx -> github_unavailable everywhere
findings.ruleCheck: tool_gateway.ToolFailed: on a write, only a status that proves nothing was created may become ToolFailed; everything else stays unknown and is reconciled. Codes are stored on receipts and asserted by tests (test_github_issues.py:147, tests/db/connector_check.py:172), so rename them only deliberately.
findings.verifierNote: Three refused sets, two UnclearReply classes, failure_for and eight except-httpx blocks in six tool modules recounted with grep.

findings.title: Six httpx client constructors use different defaults, and the GitHub token client honors proxy environment variables

locations.note: Token client without trust_env=False; 15 s
trust_env=False, no redirects, 20 s
trust_env=False, no timeout (httpx's 5 s) under a 20 s cap
trust_env left at the default; 15 s
trust_env left at the default; a new client per operation for a process-wide key; 30 s
trust_env=False; 10 s
The store is built at startup but opens a client per call

findings.evidence:
Abridged:
```
return httpx.AsyncClient(base_url=base_url, headers=dict(headers), transport=transport,
    timeout=seconds, follow_redirects=False, trust_env=False)                  # provider_http.py:51-58
return httpx.AsyncClient(base_url=API_URL, transport=transport, timeout=_REQUEST_SECONDS,
    follow_redirects=False, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}", ...})  # github_issues.py:128-138
```
openrouter_metadata.http_client and SupabaseObjectStore._client also leave trust_env at httpx's default of True. Timeouts are 20, 15, 15, 30 and 10 seconds plus httpx's 5-second default, and none is derived from the tool's timeout_seconds.
findings.impact: The GitHub client carries a token with write scope on the repository (Decision 0022 D6) and will use whatever HTTPS_PROXY or ALL_PROXY the worker's environment sets, while the Tavily and Jina clients and the URL guard refuse the environment. The storage client's service key is process-wide, yet the client is rebuilt for every operation instead of being owned by the lifespan, as DH-06 asks. A reader can't tell which timeout bounds a given call.
findings.recommendation: Create clients through one factory with follow_redirects=False and trust_env=False fixed and a required, named timeout. Keep per-attempt clients where a per-attempt key requires them (tools, PK-01). Own one client in the API and worker lifespans for process-level credentials (storage, OpenRouter metadata). Define each timeout next to the tool timeout it must fit inside, and pin that relation in a test, as test_model_attempts.py:297-298 does for the model client.
findings.ruleCheck: DH-06: own HTTP clients in process lifecycles and bound timeouts. PK-01 keeps tool keys per attempt, so tool clients stay per attempt. The OpenRouter SDK client in models/factory.py is outside this change (model-gateway rule).
findings.verifierNote: Six constructors and their defaults confirmed; with trust_env left on, httpx 0.28.1 also reads SSL_CERT_FILE and SSL_CERT_DIR, so a proxy plus a custom CA could see the GitHub token.

findings.title: GitHub read tools resolve the target and open a new client for every request, so one call can read two repositories

locations.note: get resolves the target and opens a client per request
workflow_runs: one get for the runs plus one per failed run, up to 10
search_issues resolves the target, then get resolves it again
Each resolution reads the repository setting and loads and decrypts the token (170-181)
By contrast, one resolution and one client per attempt

findings.evidence:
```
async def get(context: ToolContext, path: str, params: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None) -> Any:
    repository, token = await attempt_target(context, environ)
    async with github_client(token, transport) as http:
        try:
            reply = await http.get(path.format(repository=repository), params=params)
```
findings.impact: In one attempt, github_list_workflow_runs makes up to 11 target resolutions (each a settings read, a credential load and a decryption) and 11 TLS connections. If the workspace's repository setting changes mid-call, the jobs come from a different repository than the runs list they annotate.
findings.recommendation: Resolve (repository, token) once per attempt and pass one open client and repository to the handler, as open_pull_request does. search_issues then uses the same resolution for its repo: qualifier. GithubConnector.attempt() from the factory-closure finding provides this.
findings.sketch:
async def list_workflow_runs(api: GithubApi, arguments) -> GithubListWorkflowRunsOutput:
    found = (await api.read(runs_path(arguments), params(arguments))).get("workflow_runs") or []
    ...   # each failed run's jobs through the same api: one repository, token and pool per call
findings.ruleCheck: PK-01 and Decision 0025 resolve the key and repository per attempt; resolving once per attempt meets that. The approved-repository pinning in attempt_target is unchanged.
findings.verifierNote: get resolves the target per request; workflow_runs makes up to 11 resolutions, each a settings read plus a credential load and decryption in tool_keys.github_target.

findings.title: Provider replies are parsed as Any with ad hoc .get chains, so malformed replies fail with different codes or crash consumers

locations.note: call returns Any; reply.get with no dict check
Checks isinstance(reply, dict)
AttributeError caught for one level only
_checked returns raw JSON; handlers index item['number'] (89)
Unvalidated dict[str, Any]; JSON errors not caught; both factories return Any
parse_catalog trusts the payload's shape
The worker's consumer catches AttributeError and TypeError
The settings path parses without that catch

findings.evidence:
Counted by grep: 15 .json() calls in 9 adapter modules, 14 in 8 without browser_executor's local DevTools reply, none checked against a declared shape.
```
items = [item for item in reply.get("results", []) if isinstance(item, dict)]   # tavily.py:68
data = reply.get("data") if isinstance(reply, dict) else None                    # jina.py:72
chart = reply.json().get("chart") or {}    # market_data.py:97
number=int(item["number"]),                # github_reads.py:89
data: dict[str, Any] = reply.json()        # openrouter_metadata.py:46
except (OSError, ValueError, TypeError, AttributeError) as error:   # worker_inference.py:99
```
findings.impact: Each module validates the trust boundary in its own way, despite DH-06's single requirement. A list where Tavily expects an object fails as the generic tool_failed, while the same shape is provider_reply_malformed from Jina's reader and an empty success from Jina search. A malformed GitHub item is retried once as tool_failed. A non-object catalog reply makes provider_settings.models raise, because only the worker's consumer catches AttributeError and TypeError.
findings.recommendation: Declare small, lenient, adapter-private Pydantic reply models with extra='ignore' and only the fields used, and parse through one helper that maps ValidationError or ValueError to ToolFailed('provider_reply_malformed') for reads. For effectful writes, a body that can't be parsed after a 201 must stay unknown (raise UnclearReply), never become ToolFailed. Make catalog_fetcher return None on malformed JSON or shape, and type both metadata factories with the existing CatalogFetcher alias and a KeyValidator alias instead of Any.
findings.ruleCheck: DH-06: validate data at trust boundaries. The reply models are adapter-private, not public contracts, so OpenAPI and the generated client are unaffected. Write semantics from tool_gateway.ToolFailed are preserved.
findings.verifierNote: Recounted 15 .json() calls in 9 modules (14 in 8 without the local CDP reply); a list reply from Jina search is an empty success rather than provider_reply_malformed, so the impact was corrected.

findings.title: LoopMiddleware._admitted_call passes state out of a nested closure through four mutable lists

locations.note: 107 lines, C901 15, 65 statements
Four out-parameter lists
The nested dispatch writes to them
_bounded appends to its caller's stopped list (423)
Lists decoded in priority order; only the last reply and ticket are read

findings.evidence:
```
limit: list[LimitReached] = []
stopped: list[str] = []
replies: list[Any] = []
last_ticket: list[Any] = []

async def dispatch(ticket: Any) -> ModelOutput:
```

    stop_code: str | None = None      # guard, run or limit stop; first wins
    ticket: Ticket | None = None
    reply: ModelResponse | None = None

async def _admitted_call(self, request, handler, remaining, route=None):
    chosen, record = route or self._route, _CallRecord()
    admission_request = await self._admission_request(chosen, request)
    try:
        output = await call_with_policy(self._admission, admission_request,

    await self._record_reply(record)
    return record.reply, output.complete
